sections.title: Name and identification
sections.text: The name accepted by Species Fungorum (Kew) in 2026 is Neoboletus erythropus (Pers.) Bertolini & Papetti; VAPKO 2023 also uses Neoboletus erythropus. The British Natural History Museum checklist uses Neoboletus luridiformis for the bolete long called Boletus erythropus sensu auct. These names reflect differing nomenclatural treatments: Boletus erythropus on its own in older guides can be ambiguous. This profile follows the current Kew and VAPKO treatment.

sections.title: Cap, pores and flesh
sections.text: This stout bolete has a convex then flattening cap, usually chestnut to very dark brown, dry and velvety when young, becoming smoother; it commonly reaches 8–20 cm. The underside consists of tubes and pores, never gills. The pores are orange at first, becoming orange-red to bright red, and may turn brown with age. The tubes are lemon-yellow to yellow-green. Both pores and tubes blue strongly when touched or cut. The firm flesh is yellow and often turns deep blue very rapidly.

sections.title: Stem: dotted, not netted
sections.text: The thick stem is usually yellow to orange-yellow and about 7–15 cm tall. It is densely covered with small reddish dots or flecks, sometimes less distinct near the top: these are separate dots, not a raised net of reticulated ridges. This helps distinguish it from red-pored boletes with netted stems, but is not enough on its own to identify a specimen. The spore print is olive-brown.

sections.title: Habitat and season
sections.text: An ectomycorrhizal woodland bolete associated especially with beech and oak, and also reported with conifers. It is often found on acidic or nutrient-poor soils, though habitat varies by region. Fruiting is mainly in summer and autumn; exact timing depends on local climate.

sections.title: Cooking and caution
sections.text: The scarletina bolete is toxic raw and may cause digestive upset if undercooked. The Canton of Geneva’s Consumer Affairs and Veterinary Service recommends cooking it for at least 15–20 minutes; slicing helps it cook evenly. Cooking cannot make an uncertain identification safe. Never eat a bolete identified only from a photograph; have a harvest checked by an expert.

sections.title: About the plate
sections.text: The plate shows four views of the same type of fruit body: a whole specimen, a lengthwise cut showing yellow flesh and blue staining, the cap from above, and the pore surface from below. The stem has separate red dots on a yellow ground, with no netting.

traits: Stout chestnut to dark brown cap, convex then flatter, dry and velvety when young
Yellow tubes; orange then bright red pores that blue when touched
Thick yellow stem with separate red dots, not a reticulated net
Firm yellow flesh that turns blue very rapidly when cut
Woodland species under broadleaved trees and sometimes conifers; mainly summer and autumn
safetyNote: Toxic raw or undercooked and may cause digestive upset. Geneva authorities recommend cooking for at least 15–20 minutes. If identification is uncertain, do not eat it; have the collection checked by an expert.
